prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and for showing how reallocation across firms creates new channels for the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting is a clear conceptual break from the representative-firm trade models. It explains exporter premia, within-industry reallocation and a new margin for gains from trade. It also moved well beyond trade into macroeconomics, productivity and industrial organisation. The central paper (Melitz 2003) and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work are more than twenty years old. They have been tested against firm-level data in many countries and are now standard in graduate training and policy evaluation. Attribution is comparatively tight for a two-person prize. Melitz supplies the core model, and Helpman supplies the broader firm-level programme and its link to exporting versus FDI. Trade has not been recognised since 2008, so timing is plausible. I judge this by the same criteria I apply to the other candidates: conceptual novelty, empirical confirmation, maturity and cleanness of credit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the Committee may see this as an extension of the new trade theory already recognised in 2008, rather than a separate discovery. Priority is also contested. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum made closely related contributions that are not among the credited names. The welfare gains in the quantitative literature depend on parametrisation and model structure. A two-name prize therefore leaves out contributors with real claims, and omitting Redding may be criticised.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B034 first and credits Melitz and Helpman for the core. She treats Redding's quantitative spatial and trade work as later and more derivative, so she leaves him out. She also flags that Krugman's 2008 prize and Helpman's separate political-economy work overlap with this candidate.
responses.response: I agree on the two-name core and on leaving Redding out. His quantitative extensions are important but build on the framework rather than founding it. I take the Krugman overlap more seriously than she does. The Committee would need to argue that selection and reallocation across firms is a distinct discovery and not an elaboration of monopolistic-competition trade. I think it is distinct. The mechanism is different, the main margin is different, and the empirical content is different. Melitz-style selection can be tested on firm-level data in a way that the earlier models could not. That distinction should be stated in the citation.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B036 first and B034 second. He worries that a trade prize already went to Krugman in 2008, that the priority question involving Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is unresolved, and that Helpman appears on another trade entry.
responses.response: The priority concern is the most serious reservation I have about B034, and I cannot dispose of it with the evidence provided. Bernard-Jensen documented the exporter facts before Melitz. Eaton-Kortum is a different modelling line, so it overlaps only in part. Melitz still supplied the tractable general-equilibrium model that organised those facts and drove the later work. I would credit him with that integration rather than with the empirical facts. I take his point on Helpman being on another trade ballot. For this ballot, his credit rests on the heterogeneous-firm work itself, so I do not think the overlap undermines the case. I do not accept that the 2008 prize reduces the case, because the later work is conceptually different.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B036 first. She argues that it combines a clear explanatory framework with credible quasi-experimental evidence and that the China-shock results have held up. She proposes Autor, Katz and Hanson and recognises that omitting Dorn is a real cost.
responses.response: She and Boppart have persuaded me on attribution. The China-shock evidence is most cleanly credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Katz's contribution is the earlier skill-premium and technology strand, which is a distinct achievement. My opening Autor-Katz pairing split the two strands without fully crediting either. If B036 were the preferred achievement, I would now propose Autor, Dorn and Hanson for the trade-shock work. I still keep B034 ahead. Its credit structure is cleaner, and the trade-shock literature is still debating magnitudes and persistence. I do not treat the number of first-place votes as evidence of scientific merit. I do treat B036 as the strongest alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats heterogeneous-firm trade as a distinct discovery or as a refinement of the new trade theory recognised in 2008.
How to credit the Bernard-Jensen empirical precursors and Eaton-Kortum, who are outside the credited names.
How sensitive the quantitative welfare gains are to parametrisation, which affects how strongly the citation can speak to the size of the gains.
Whether B036 should be preferred if the Committee accepts the clean Autor-Dorn-Hanson attribution and judges the persistence debate to be settled enough.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My adjunct post at Chicago Booth and my co-authorships (Kaplan, Axelson, Weisbach and others) do not connect to the credited names on B034, B036 or B020. My field is corporate finance, and B012 is the only neighbouring candidate, so I have tried to apply the same criteria across fields.
